2	// scheduler is doing, published as a static site.
3	//
4	// WHY A PACK AND NOT ENGINE CODE. The dashboard is not part of running the scheduler:
5	// nothing converges, scheduler runs or executes because it exists, and a member that never
6	// looks at it should not carry it. Engine code is what every member runs; this is
7	// content a member OPTS INTO, and adoptable content in this corpus is a pack. That

9	// migration lane, a declaration that gates it, and an adoption moment at which its
10	// deployment can be wired.
11	//
12	// WHAT IT READS. Only the queue's own vocabulary and the task declarations at HEAD,
13	// through the tasks pack's published `shared-code/`, so the page cannot drift from the
14	// mechanism it renders. Those relative paths resolve identically in the canon (`packs/<id>/`
15	// beside its siblings) and in a member's mount (`.claudinite/shared/packs/<id>/`), which is
16	// why the pack can be read straight out of the mount with nothing rewritten.
17	//
18	// NO PROSE. There is no way to write the dashboard wrongly in a consuming repo — it is
19	// a page, not a practice — and prose here would cost every session in every declaring
20	// repo tokens for something no session acts on. Its README carries the explanation
21	// instead and `prose` stays null.

25	// what it has to say; its values come either from its own generated file in the
26	// member's tree or from one of the two platform facts the page already reads for every

28	// page's OWN reader accepts, which the JSON Schema beside it structurally cannot,

1 claudinite-dashboard 2 3 A read-only view of what a repo's — or a fleet's — Claudinite is doing: what is stuck, 4 what is queued, what has run, and what the corpus has been costing and catching. 5 6 **Two modes, and a deployment states which one it is.** `mode` is `"repo"` — that 7 repo's own page — or `"fleet"` — the overview across a roster. It is the one key with 8 **no default**: the build refuses to publish a deployment that did not say, and refuses 9 a mode that contradicts the rest of the config (`fleet` naming no roster source, 10 `repo` naming one). 11 12 It used to be inferred: a config that named where more than one member came from was a 13 fleet, and silence was a repo page. That reads fine until a fleet deployment loses its 14 roster source — a dropped key, a renamed artifact, an enumeration that was never 15 configured — and publishes a one-repo dashboard that looks entirely intentional. An 16 inference cannot tell "this repo only" from "the fleet, whose members went missing"; 17 a stated mode can, and the disagreement becomes a failed build instead of a quietly 18 wrong site. 19 20 **Opt-in.** Nothing fingerprints it and `--init` never seeds it: a repo carries this 21 because someone declared it. Adopting it wires the GitHub Pages deploy. 22 23 ## Adopting it 24 25 ```jsonc 26 // .claudinite-settings.json 27 { "packs": ["claudinite-dashboard"] } 28 ``` 29 30 That is the whole of it for a member: the dashboard covers this repo, signs in with a 31 pasted token, and publishes to Pages. Adoption seeds 32 [the deploy workflow](stubs/workflows/claudinite-dashboard-pages.yml) into 33 `.github/workflows/`, and **you must enable Pages with source *GitHub Actions*** — a 34 repository setting no Action can flip; until then the deploy job is the only thing 35 that fails. 36 37 Everything else is optional `config` on the declaration: 38 39 | Key | Default | What it buys | 40 |---|---|---| 41 | `mode` | **none — required** | `"repo"` or `"fleet"`. The build fails without it, and fails when it disagrees with the roster keys below | 42 | `owner` | — | Whose repos this deployment covers. The page **enumerates them in the browser, as the viewer** — so this is a fleet deployment, and the fleet a person sees is exactly the fleet they can read. The way to build a fleet dashboard | 43 | `exclude` | none | Repos under that owner that are not members (either `owner/name` or the bare name). Archived and forked repos leave by their own state | 44 | `repos` | — | An explicit member list instead, for a deployment that wants a fixed set | 45 | `rosterFile` | — | A generated artifact in the repo listing members — the legacy shape, still read | 46 | `canonRepo` | — | The repo whose live engine and pack versions member stamps are compared against; unset means freshness reads *unknown* rather than being guessed | 47 | `clientId`, `exchangeUrl` | — | Both together turn on **Sign in with GitHub**; either alone does nothing | 48 | `redirectUri` | the page's URL | Override when the callback differs | 49 | `defaultRepo` | this repo | Which repo a single-repo deployment shows | 50 51 ## Why a pack and not engine code 52 53 Nothing converges, scheduler runs or executes because the dashboard exists, and a member that 54 never looks at it should not carry it. Engine code is what every member *runs*; this 55 is content a member opts into. Being a pack also buys it a version and migration 56 lane, a declaration that gates it, and an adoption moment at which the deploy can be 57 wired — none of which engine code has. 58 59 It has **two views**, and which one you land on is the URL: 60 61 - **Fleet** — every member at once, worst first. What a deployment with a roster 62 opens on. 63 - **Repo** — one member's scheduler in full. Reached by clicking a member, or 64 `?repo=owner/name` directly. 65 66 A deployment with one member (or none) goes straight to the repo view: a one-row 67 fleet overview would be nothing but a click in the way. 68 69 ## Running it locally 70 71 ```sh 72 node packs/claudinite-dashboard/serve.mjs missingbulb/Claudinite 73 ``` 74 75 ## Two kinds of data, read two different ways 76 77 Everything on both pages is one of two things, and the difference is the whole reason 78 the page can afford what it shows. 79 80 **What is true right now** is a live read, and there are few of them: the repo, its 81 head commit, one page of issues, one page of Actions runs. All are ETag-revalidated, 82 and a `304` costs no rate-limit budget at all. 83 84 **What happened before** is one file: the repo's own 85 `.claudinite/local/usage.GENERATED.json`, folded hourly by the 86 [usage-fold task](../claudinite-tasks/tasks/usage-fold/README.md) in the 87 claudinite-growth pack. It is content at a sha, so it is read once when the default 88 branch moves and **not at all** while it has not. Reaching a month back over the API 89 instead would be a paginated crawl per repo per load, which is exactly the shape this 90 client is built to avoid. 91 92 Measured against a stubbed API, one repo with five declared tasks: 93 94 | | Requests | Of those, free | 95 |---|---|---| 96 | Cold (empty cache) | 14 | 0 | 97 | Warm (same head sha) | 5 | **5** — every one a `304`, nothing spent | 98 99 So a warm reload of a repo page costs **nothing** against the viewer's budget. 100 101 The two freshnesses are reported separately in the footer, because they are not the 102 same: the live half is as fresh as this load, the past half as fresh as the repo's last 103 fold. A page that showed one timestamp for both would be claiming the older half is as 104 current as the newer. 105 106 A repo that does not fold the file is a normal state, not a fault: the panels that 107 wanted it say so, and nothing else on the page is affected. 108 109 ## What the repo page shows 110 111 | Panel | Answers | 112 |---|---| 113 | **Start here** | The one piece of work most worth doing in this repo, named with the issue to open and what it costs you — the top row of the same ranking the work table is ordered by | 114 | **At a glance** | Minutes waiting on a person and what they are made of, items parked, open pull requests and issues, CI on the default branch, runs in flight, stars, and drift against the canon | 115 | **Work** | One row per piece of work, in three views — **stuck** (what has stopped, and for how long), **pending** (what is moving, and what happens next), **all** (what each task is and what it has done). The page opens on the worst view that has anything in it | 116 | **What the queue closed** | Per-day outcomes over a fortnight — today from the live issue page, the days before it from the fold | 117 | **What ran** | 48 hours of scheduler runs, executor runs and agent sessions per hour; hovering an hour names the tasks that executed in it | 118 | **What Claudinite is doing here** | 30 days of rule tokens against checks executed, on two stated scales — plus tokens spent, lines committed and releases where the fold carries them | 119 | **What the packs report** | One card per declared pack that contributes — see [below](#what-a-pack-contributes). Last, because it is the only region whose contents differ from repo to repo | 120 121 ### One table, not two 122 123 The roster and the queue used to be separate tables, and they were the same rows 124 twice: a task's row could not say what its item was doing without repeating the item 125 table, and an item's row could not say what it was *for* without repeating the roster. 126 Worse, the reader had to join them by eye to answer the question they opened the page 127 with — is anything stuck. 128 129 So there is one row per piece of work and the **view decides which rows and which 130 columns**. The three views are three genuinely different questions, which is why they 131 do not share a column set. Switching between them moves the rows rather than redrawing 132 them, so the row you were reading stays findable; a reader who has asked their platform 133 for less motion gets the repaint and none of the movement. 134 ... - adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.

Rebasing (1/4)Rebasing (2/4)Rebasing (3/4)Rebasing (4/4)[KSuccessfully rebased and updated refs/heads/claude/oauth-exchange-lifecycle-apn3by.
The four steps, in the order they unblock each other. Adoption files them as a tracking
issue rather than leaving them here to be met after the first anonymous viewer gives up.

1. **Register a GitHub App** with read-only **Contents**, **Issues** and **Actions**, and
   *Request user authorization (OAuth) during installation* enabled. The callback URL is
   the deployed page — or the `https://<user>.github.io/` root with **wildcard matching**,
   which covers every project Pages site on that host. Note the client id, generate a
   client secret.
2. **Install it** on the account holding the repos the dashboard reads. Per *account*, not
   per repo: a user token reaches only what the app is installed on, so an uninstalled
   account renders every member row as *not visible to you*.
3. **Set the repository variable `CLAUDINITE_DASHBOARD_CLIENT_ID`**, and **deploy
   [`oauth-exchange.mjs`](oauth-exchange.mjs)** by running this pack's
   [`deploy-oauth-exchange`](tasks/deploy-oauth-exchange/README.md) task — it uploads the
   endpoint to Cloudflare Workers, proves the URL answers, and reports it. One deployment
   serves every dashboard the same owner runs.
4. **Set `CLAUDINITE_DASHBOARD_EXCHANGE_URL`** to the URL that run reported. The client id
   alone does nothing — the pair is what makes the button appear.

Both are repository variables (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → **Variables**),
not config and not secrets: they are what you set while standing in the App's settings, the
second is minted by a deploy rather than authored, and neither is confidential — the client
id is in every authorize URL and the exchange URL is fetched by the browser.

Done when a signed-in viewer's rate pill reads `…/5000 · user`.

### Why "just use my existing GitHub login" is not on that list

content.text:
[#1532](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1532) is merged and captured. On #1465: **no, it didn't** — and I've now put it there, so it's worth a fresh look rather than the conditional LGTM.

The generic instruction is the thing you just merged: `adopt-pack` now points at `writing-handover-issues` for how to write the adoption issue. That was never in #1465, by design of the split.

But your question surfaced something the split had hidden. The dashboard pack's own `adoptionHandover` entries are the *source material* an adopting session renders into that issue — and they were exactly what the new skill rejects:

```
Before                                   After
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
"…(Settings → Pages)"                    "— this repo's /settings/pages"
  a breadcrumb where a link belongs

A 90-word sign-in step: register an      A one-line decision that points at the
App, install it, set a variable, run     README's "Turning sign-in on", which is
the task, set another variable, plus     now the checklist — 12 boxes, deep paths,
a rationale — rendered as ONE checkbox   and the two once-shown values saying so
```

The README section that step points at was four numbered paragraphs; it's now the checklist a person can work, with the per-account install rule, wildcard matching and the variables-not-secrets reasoning moved below the boxes.

One thing worth telling you plainly: **the test guarding that step was worthless.** It asserted the step named both variable names — which the 90-word paragraph satisfied perfectly. It now asserts the step points at the checklist and stays under a word bound, and I watched it fail on a deliberately re-inflated step. A second, older assertion in the same test earned its keep: my first rewrite dropped the "leave it on the token box" answer, and it caught that immediately — so the do-nothing option is still stated as an answer.

Full suite 2862/2862, `check_the_work` clean, `check_the_world` 0 blocking, rebased on the merged `main`.

Two things I did not do, both offered rather than assumed:

- **`writing-handover-issues` said "no check" and I now think that was half-wrong.** Issue bodies aren't repo files — but `adoptionHandover` steps are, and a word bound over every pack's is deterministic and corpus-wide. The word-count guard I just wrote is local to this pack's test, which is the copy that should be a check. That belongs in basics, not here, so it's a separate change.
- **No production verification for #1532.** Its effect is on how future sessions write issues; nothing observable goes live, and the bar for spending your attention isn't met.

> ⚠️ Still open: [#1465](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1465) needs a fresh look — the handover instruction you asked about wasn't there, so I added it as the last commit rather than merging on the conditional LGTM. Offered separately: promoting the handover-step word bound from this pack's test into a basics check.
